     1  /-
     2  Copyright (c) 2019 Chris Hughes. All rights reserved.

     6  module
     7  
     8  public import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Basis.VectorSpace
     9  public import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Dimension.Free
    10  public import Mathlib.RingTheory.SimpleRing.Basic
    11  
    12  /-!
    13  # Finite-dimensional vector spaces
    14  
    15  This file defines finite-dimensional vector spaces and shows our definition is equivalent to
    16  alternative definitions.
    17  
    18  ## Main definitions
    19  
    20  Assume `V` is a vector space over a division ring `K`. There are (at least) three equivalent
    21  definitions of finite-dimensionality of `V`:
    22  
    23  - it admits a finite basis.
    24  - it is finitely generated.
    25  - it is Noetherian, i.e., every subspace is finitely generated.
    26  
    27  We introduce a typeclass `FiniteDimensional K V` capturing this property. For ease of transfer of
    28  proof, it is defined using the second point of view, i.e., as `Module.Finite`. However, we prove
    29  that all these points of view are equivalent, with the following lemmas
    30  (in the namespace `FiniteDimensional`):
    31  
    32  - `Module.finBasis` and `Module.finBasisOfFinrankEq`
    33    are bases for finite-dimensional vector spaces, where the index type
    34    is `Fin` (in `Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Dimension/Free.lean`)
    35  - `fintypeBasisIndex` states that a finite-dimensional
    36    vector space has a finite basis
    37  - `Module.Basis.finiteDimensional_of_finite` states that the existence of a basis indexed by a
    38    finite type implies finite-dimensionality
    39  - `of_finite_basis` states that the existence of a basis indexed by a
    40    finite set implies finite-dimensionality
    41  - `of_finrank_pos` states that a nonzero `finrank` (implying non-infinite dimension)
    42    implies finite-dimensionality
    43  - `IsNoetherian.iff_fg` states that the space is finite-dimensional if and only if
    44    it is Noetherian (in `Mathlib/FieldTheory/Finiteness.lean`)
    45  
    46  We make use of `finrank`, the dimension of a finite-dimensional space, returning a `Nat`, as
    47  opposed to `Module.rank`, which returns a `Cardinal`. When the space has infinite dimension, its
    48  `finrank` is by convention set to `0`. `finrank` is not defined using `FiniteDimensional`.
    49  For basic results that do not need the `FiniteDimensional` class, import
    50  `Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Dimension/Finrank.lean`.
"}]

     6  module
     7  
     8  public import Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.Projection.Basic

    10  /-!
    11  # Subspaces associated with orthogonal projections
    12  
    13  Here, the orthogonal projection is used to prove a series of more subtle lemmas about the
    14  orthogonal complement of subspaces of `E` (the orthogonal complement itself was
    15  defined in `Mathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/Orthogonal.lean`) such that they admit
    16  orthogonal projections; the lemma
    17  `Submodule.sup_orthogonal_of_hasOrthogonalProjection`,
    18  stating that for a subspace `K` of `E` such that `K` admits an orthogonal projection we have
    19  `K ⊔ Kᗮ = ⊤`, is a typical example.
    20  -/
    21  
    22  public section
    23  
    24  variable {𝕜 E F : Type*} [RCLike 𝕜]
    25  variable [NormedAddCommGroup E] [NormedAddCommGroup F]
    26  variable [InnerProductSpace 𝕜 E] [InnerProductSpace ℝ F]
    27  
    28  local notation "⟪" x ", " y "⟫" => inner 𝕜 x y

    30  variable (K : Submodule 𝕜 E)
    31  
    32  namespace Submodule
    33  
    34  /-- If `K₁` admits an orthogonal projection and is contained in `K₂`,
    35  then `K₁` and `K₁ᗮ ⊓ K₂` span `K₂`. -/

    37      [K₁.HasOrthogonalProjection] : K₁ ⊔ K₁ᗮ ⊓ K₂ = K₂ := by
    38    ext x
    39    rw [Submodule.mem_sup]
    40    let v : K₁ := orthogonalProjectionOnto K₁ x
    41    have hvm : x - v ∈ K₁ᗮ := sub_starProjection_mem_orthogonal x
    42    constructor
    43    · rintro ⟨y, hy, z, hz, rfl⟩
    44      exact K₂.add_mem (h hy) hz.2

    48  /-- If `K` admits an orthogonal projection, then `K` and `Kᗮ` span the whole space. -/

    50    convert Submodule.sup_orthogonal_inf_of_hasOrthogonalProjection (le_top : K ≤ ⊤)

    56  theorem orthogonal_orthogonal [K.HasOrthogonalProjection] : Kᗮᗮ = K := by

    13  /-!
    14  # Inner product spaces
    15  
    16  This file defines inner product spaces.
    17  Hilbert spaces can be obtained using the set of assumptions
    18  `[RCLike 𝕜] [NormedAddCommGroup E] [InnerProductSpace 𝕜 E] [CompleteSpace E]`.
    19  For convenience, a variable alias `HilbertSpace` is provided so that one can write
    20  `variable? [HilbertSpace 𝕜 E]` and get this as a suggestion.
    21  
    22  An inner product space is a vector space endowed with an inner product. It generalizes the notion of
    23  dot product in `ℝ^n` and provides the means of defining the length of a vector and the angle between
    24  two vectors. In particular vectors `x` and `y` are orthogonal if their inner product equals zero.
    25  We define both the real and complex cases at the same time using the `RCLike` typeclass.
    26  
    27  Rather than defining the norm on an inner product space to be `√(re ⟪x, x⟫)`, we assume that a norm
    28  is given, and add a hypothesis stating that `‖x‖ ^ 2 = re ⟪x, x⟫`. This makes it possible to
    29  handle spaces where the norm is equal, but not defeq, to the square root of the
    30  inner product. Defining a norm starting from an inner product is handled via the
    31  `InnerProductSpace.Core` structure.
    32  
    33  This file is intended to contain the minimal amount of machinery needed to define inner product
    34  spaces, and to construct a normed space from an inner product space. Many more general lemmas can
    35  be found in `Analysis.InnerProductSpace.Basic`. For the specific construction of an inner product
    36  structure on `n → 𝕜` for `𝕜 = ℝ` or `ℂ`, see `EuclideanSpace` in
    37  `Analysis.InnerProductSpace.PiL2`.
    38  
    39  ## Main results
    40  
    41  - We define the class `InnerProductSpace 𝕜 E` extending `NormedSpace 𝕜 E` with a number of basic
    42    properties, most notably the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Here `𝕜` is understood to be either `ℝ`
    43    or `ℂ`, through the `RCLike` typeclass.
    44  
    45  ## Notation
    46  
    47  We globally denote the real and complex inner products by `⟪·, ·⟫_ℝ` and `⟪·, ·⟫_ℂ` respectively.
    48  We also provide two notation namespaces: `RealInnerProductSpace`, `ComplexInnerProductSpace`,
    49  which respectively introduce the plain notation `⟪·, ·⟫` for the real and complex inner product.
    50
